network.overall_strategy: Threonine is reached by two literature-backed endgames: a surface cyanosulfidic Strecker branch from lactaldehyde and a hydrothermal aldol-type homologation of alanine with formaldehyde. Alanine is supplied either by surface acetaldehyde-derived Strecker chemistry or by hydrothermal reduction of serine. To keep the graph atom-balanced and mechanistically explicit, aminonitrile hydrolysis is decomposed into amide formation plus amide hydrolysis, and the lactaldehyde branch includes both the Patel-style stepwise sequence and a plausible net one-pot Strecker alternative. Nodes are written without stereochemistry because prebiotic threonine would be racemic, no unsupported catalyst is imposed, and the 10 listed pathways intentionally include both full feedstock routes and shorter entry routes from plausible accumulated intermediates within the same connected network.

reactions.name: HCN addition to lactaldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic cyanosulfidic surface pool or evaporitic shoreline; wet-dry concentration helps HCN activity; UV is important upstream for feedstock generation but not required during the addition step.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to the aldehyde carbonyl of lactaldehyde, followed by protonation of the alkoxide to give the cyanohydrin.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) experimentally support the lactaldehyde-derived cyanosulfidic threonine sequence. HCN addition to an aldehyde is the expected first step. Lactaldehyde availability is a real open question noted in the review, so this node is conditioned on local production or concentration of lactaldehyde. The intermediate is written here as the chemically conserved C4 cyanohydrin required by lactaldehyde plus HCN.

reactions.name: Amination of lactaldehyde cyanohydrin

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous surface phase with dissolved NH3; intermittent concentration by evaporation is favorable.

reactions.mechanism: Strecker-type amination of the cyanohydrin center generates the aminonitrile and expels water.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by the aminonitrile-forming threonine branch in Patel et al. (2015). Ammonia converts the cyanohydrin to the alpha-aminonitrile under mild aqueous surface conditions. The review notes that aminonitrile stability under UV and fluctuating pH remains uncertain.

reactions.name: Net Strecker conversion of lactaldehyde to threonine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic cyanosulfidic pool; included as a net alternative to the separated cyanohydrin and amination steps.

reactions.mechanism: Net Strecker condensation through transient cyanohydrin and/or iminium intermediates gives the aminonitrile directly.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) support the same chemistry as a stepwise sequence. This node is the chemically reasonable net Strecker condensation of lactaldehyde, HCN, and NH3 to the threonine aminonitrile; it is included as an alternative pathway but is more speculative than the separated rxn_001 plus rxn_002 representation.

reactions.name: Hydration of threonine aminonitrile to threoninamide

conditions.other: Wet surface phase after concentration; dark or shielded intervals help preserve labile nitriles.

reactions.mechanism: Water adds to the nitrile carbon and tautomerizes to the corresponding amide.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) report net hydrolysis of the threonine aminonitrile to threonine. The explicit amide node is a mechanistic unpacking of that net result, since nitrile hydrolysis normally proceeds through an amide; the threonine-specific amide was not the main isolated product in the cited study.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of threoninamide to threonine

conditions.other: Repeated wet phases and mild heating favor amide hydrolysis; strongly prolonged UV exposure is unfavorable.

reactions.mechanism: Amide hydrolysis converts the carboxamide to the amino acid with liberation of ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Completes the Patel et al. (2015) nitrile-to-amino-acid sequence. Wet phases and mild heating favor amide hydrolysis to threonine, whereas prolonged UV exposure at the surface would tend to erode yields.

reactions.name: Hydrothermal homologation of alanine with formaldehyde

conditions.other: Subseafloor or vent-margin hydrothermal water; H2-rich and anoxic; rapid quenching or cooler margins favor product survival.

reactions.mechanism: Aldol-type homologation in which the alpha-carbon of alanine adds to formaldehyde, forming a new C-C bond and the beta-hydroxylated amino acid.
reactions.reasoning: Aubrey, Cleaves, and Bada (2008) experimentally showed alanine plus formaldehyde yields threonine under submarine hydrothermal conditions. This direct homologation is strong literature support, but the review highlights open questions about formaldehyde concentration, threonine versus allo-threonine selectivity, and threonine survival at higher vent temperatures. The node is written without stereochemistry because prebiotic products would be racemic.

reactions.name: HCN addition to acetaldehyde

conditions.other: Anoxic cyanide-bearing surface pool with intermittent concentration.

reactions.mechanism: Cyanide adds to acetaldehyde to give its cyanohydrin, lactonitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) place alanine in the same aldehyde-determined cyanosulfidic amino-acid family, so acetaldehyde is expected to enter through the standard cyanohydrin step. This first transformation is chemically well precedented even though the review emphasizes the downstream aminonitrile and amino acid more than isolated lactonitrile.

reactions.name: Amination of lactonitrile to alanine aminonitrile

conditions.other: Anoxic aqueous surface phase with dissolved NH3 and episodic evaporation.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonolysis converts the cyanohydrin alcohol center to the aminonitrile, with water as the net leaving product.
reactions.reasoning: Consistent with the Strecker-type amination logic used across the Patel et al. (2015) cyanosulfidic network. Ammonia converts acetaldehyde-derived lactonitrile to 2-aminopropanenitrile, the direct nitrile precursor of alanine.

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of alanine aminonitrile to alanine

conditions.other: Wet surface phase after concentration; net aminonitrile hydrolysis to the amino acid. Coefficients are inferred, so two waters are consumed overall.

reactions.mechanism: Net nitrile hydrolysis via the corresponding amide to yield alanine and ammonia.
reactions.reasoning: Patel et al. (2015) and general Strecker chemistry support hydrolysis of 2-aminopropanenitrile to alanine. In this graph it is represented as the net aminonitrile-to-amino-acid conversion; stoichiometrically two waters are consumed overall, but coefficients are inferred from composition.

reactions.name: Hydrothermal reduction of serine to alanine

conditions.other: Anoxic H2-rich vent or subseafloor setting; mineral surfaces may buffer redox, but no specific catalyst is imposed here.

reactions.mechanism: Net reductive deoxygenation of serine's side-chain hydroxymethyl group to a methyl group, yielding alanine.
reactions.reasoning: Aubrey, Cleaves, and Bada (2008) reported serine-to-alanine reduction under submarine hydrothermal conditions. H2 is included explicitly here as the balanced reducing equivalent, consistent with H2-rich vent fluids. The review also notes that amino acids can decompose at higher temperatures, so cooler vent margins or rapid quenching are favored.

pathways.name: Late-stage threoninamide hydrolysis
pathways.description: Entry route from a surface pool already containing threoninamide; simple wet-phase hydrolysis yields threonine.

pathways.name: Threonine aminonitrile to threonine via amide
pathways.description: Entry route from accumulated threonine aminonitrile; hydration gives threoninamide and subsequent hydrolysis yields threonine.

pathways.name: Cyanohydrin amination and hydrolysis route
pathways.description: Entry route from lactaldehyde cyanohydrin in an ammonia-rich surface pool, followed by aminonitrile formation and two-stage hydrolysis.

pathways.name: Full stepwise lactaldehyde surface route
pathways.description: Complete Patel-style cyanosulfidic sequence from lactaldehyde through cyanohydrin, aminonitrile, and amide to threonine.

pathways.name: Net one-pot lactaldehyde Strecker route
pathways.description: Alternative surface route in which lactaldehyde, HCN, and NH3 form threonine aminonitrile in one net Strecker event before hydrolysis to threonine.

pathways.name: Direct hydrothermal alanine homologation
pathways.description: Alanine reacts directly with formaldehyde in a hydrothermal setting to give threonine.

pathways.name: Alanine aminonitrile hydrolysis then homologation
pathways.description: Surface hydrolysis of alanine aminonitrile yields alanine, which is then delivered to hydrothermal conditions for formaldehyde homologation.

pathways.name: Lactonitrile route then homologation
pathways.description: Lactonitrile is aminated to alanine aminonitrile, hydrolyzed to alanine, and then homologated hydrothermally with formaldehyde to give threonine.

pathways.name: Acetaldehyde Strecker to alanine then homologation
pathways.description: Acetaldehyde enters surface Strecker chemistry to alanine, after which alanine is physically transferred to a hydrothermal setting for formaldehyde homologation.

pathways.name: Serine reduction to alanine then homologation
pathways.description: Hydrothermal amino-acid interconversion route in which serine is reduced to alanine and then homologated with formaldehyde to yield threonine.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A valid late-stage conversion from threoninamide to threonine. Amide hydrolysis is chemically standard, but under a generic surface setting the kinetics are under-specified; the pathway would be stronger with explicit wet-dry, warm, or prolonged aqueous hydrolysis conditions.
suggestions: Specify hydrolysis-promoting surface conditions such as wet-dry cycling, mild heating, or long aqueous residence times.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The nitrile-to-amide-to-amino-acid sequence is mechanistically sensible and conserves atoms. The main weakness is not the chemistry itself but the lack of explicit activating conditions for both hydrolysis steps in the stated surface environment.
suggestions: Add a brief rationale for how aminonitrile and amide hydrolysis proceed in the surface setting.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a good Patel-style late branch from the cyanohydrin. The amination step is literature-aligned and the downstream hydrolysis logic is coherent, though the hydrolysis segment would benefit from more explicit surface conditions.
suggestions: State whether hydrolysis is supported by wet-dry cycling, warming, or extended reaction times.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is the strongest surface route and the best match to the Patel et al. logic: cyanohydrin formation, amination, then hydrolysis to threonine. The network stays connected and chemically reasonable; the main remaining weakness is that the split nitrile and amide hydrolysis steps are plausible but lightly conditioned.
suggestions: Annotate the hydrolysis conditions more explicitly.
If available, tie the hydrolysis segment to wet-dry or warm aqueous surface phases.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The net Strecker version is chemically reasonable and balance-correct, but it is less directly evidenced than the explicitly stepwise cyanohydrin-plus-amination sequence. It works best as a condensed representation of the better-supported surface branch.
suggestions: Clarify that rxn_003 is a net shorthand for the more explicitly documented stepwise route.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A strong hydrothermal endgame consistent with Aubrey et al.: alanine homologation with formaldehyde to threonine. The main caveats are known literature issues of selectivity and possible threonine instability at hydrothermal temperatures, not a clear defect in the stated reaction.
suggestions: Note possible threonine and allo-threonine mixtures and the thermal lability of threonine under prolonged hydrothermal exposure.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The route is chemically plausible, but rxn_009 is not balanced as written and should be corrected to alanine aminonitrile + 2 H2O -> alanine + NH3 or expanded through an alaninamide intermediate. The shift from surface hydrolysis to hydrothermal homologation is plausible, but transport or shared-reservoir logic is only implicit.
suggestions: Correct rxn_009 stoichiometry to include the second water.
For consistency with the threonine branch, consider splitting rxn_009 into amide formation and amide hydrolysis.
Explicitly justify transport or accumulation linking surface alanine to hydrothermal formaldehyde chemistry.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a reasonable alanine-supply route feeding the hydrothermal homologation step. The concrete correction needed is rxn_009, which omits one water in the overall aminonitrile hydrolysis; cross-environment transfer is plausible but should be described more explicitly.
suggestions: Fix rxn_009 stoichiometry or split it into amide-forming and amide-hydrolysis steps.
Add an explicit environmental handoff rationale for alanine entering the hydrothermal setting.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A coherent multi-step route from acetaldehyde to threonine via alanine. The surface Strecker chemistry is strong and the hydrothermal endgame is literature-backed. The main defect is rxn_009, which needs one additional water for correct overall hydrolysis stoichiometry; the surface-to-hydrothermal handoff is also implicit rather than modeled.
suggestions: Correct rxn_009 to alanine aminonitrile + 2 H2O -> alanine + NH3.
Model or justify how alanine accumulated at the surface reaches the hydrothermal setting.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A compact hydrothermal route in line with the reported alanine-threonine interconversion network. The main uncertainty is rxn_010: serine-to-alanine reduction is literature-motivated, but the network would be stronger if the reductive conditions or mineral mediation behind the use of H2 were made explicit.
suggestions: Clarify the reductive chemistry for rxn_010, including whether mineral mediation is assumed.
If available, cite the specific hydrothermal conditions supporting serine reduction.

evaluation.network_feedback: This is a good, connected synthesis network with sufficient nodes, consistent IDs, and no unbalanceable reactions. The strongest parts are the Patel-style lactaldehyde surface branch and the Aubrey-style alanine plus formaldehyde hydrothermal endgame, both of which are broadly literature-aligned; omission of stereochemistry is appropriate for racemic prebiotic threonine. The main corrective issue is rxn_009, which is only balanceable if written as mol_013 + 2 mol_001 -> mol_014 + mol_002, or if expanded via an alaninamide intermediate, so the alanine branch is stoichiometrically incomplete as written. Additional weaknesses are under-specified conditions for rxn_004 and rxn_005 hydrolysis, implicit rather than explicit surface-to-hydrothermal transfer in P7-P9, and the need for clearer reductive justification for rxn_010. Literature alignment is generally good, but the network does not explicitly discuss known challenges such as lactaldehyde availability, threonine thermal lability in hydrothermal systems, and possible threonine versus allo-threonine mixtures. Overall this is a good network, but it remains below the 0.9 approval threshold.
